title: Do Language Models Share Your Doctor’s Priorities? Measuring Values from Clinical Decisions
claim: Reasonable decisions force trade-offs between competing values, and both human experts and models split sharply over which option to choose.
layout: Single tall panel, top-to-bottom rows, split orange/blue halves, bottom spectrum axis
description: A tall figure split vertically into an orange left half (Choice 1) and a blue right half (Choice 2), with row labels on a left sidebar. The top row is a text box holding a clinical vignette about a psychiatric emergency. Below it are two choice cards: a 72-hour involuntary hold, and discharge with a follow-up plan. Under each choice are four pills for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence and justice, colored green when the choice promotes the value and red when it violates it. A human row shows physician counts, 11 of 25 for Choice 1 and 14 of 25 for Choice 2. The bottom row places LLM logo chips along a horizontal axis from 10/0 to 0/10 decisions out of 10 samples. The chips cluster at both ends, showing the models are polarized.
caption: \textbf{\name{} is an instrument to measure value priorities from clinical decisions.} Each \name{} case presents a binary choice between mutually exclusive clinical actions, with each option annotated with its relationship to Principlist values. In this psychiatric emergency example, choosing involuntary hold promotes (in green) nonmaleficence and beneficence, and violates (in red) autonomy and justice. Model position along the horizontal axis shows how often each option was selected out of repeated queries using stochastic decoding at temperature 1.0. Physicians and frontier LLMs alike are sharply divided.
abstract: Clinical decisions often require weighing autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. Reasonable physicians may prioritize these values differently, yet the values that language models bring to medical advice remain poorly characterized. We introduce ValuePrism, an instrument for measuring value priorities from clinical decisions. ValuePrism combines a benchmark of 50 clinical dilemmas, each reviewed by two physicians, with an attribution method that estimates relative value priorities from choices between medically reasonable recommendations. Each case presents a clinical vignette and two mutually exclusive recommendations designed so that choosing one necessarily promotes certain values at the expense of others. Applying the instrument to frontier language models and a US-based physician panel, we find that models frequently acknowledge values favoring both recommendations but make highly consistent decisions across repeated queries, even on cases that sharply divide physicians. The ValuePrism attribution method shows that both physicians and language models express differentiated value priorities. Collectively, model values exhibit substantial diversity and most tend to fall within the physician-panel reference range. Nevertheless, a single model deployed unchecked would amplify its particular values to patients at scale. ValuePrism provides a common basis for measuring and comparing the clinical value priorities expressed by language models and physicians. Data and code are available at https://github.com/payalchandak/value-prism.
